items.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch and pH
items.contentHtml:
Henderson-Hasselbalch formula

  • pH = 6.1 + log ([bicarbonate] / (0.03 × PaCO2 in mmHg)).
  • The constant 6.1 is the pKa of carbonic acid; 0.03 is the solubility coefficient of CO2 in plasma at 37°C.
  • Key relationship: pH is determined by the bicarbonate/PaCO2 ratio, not by absolute values; normal 20:1 (bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, PaCO2 40 mmHg).
  • Primary changes: if bicarbonate decreases → metabolic acidosis; if PaCO2 increases → respiratory acidosis; opposites in alkalosis.
  • The formula does not distinguish primary compensation disorder; requires clinical and blood gas context.
  • Examination trap: in lactic acidosis, the elevated anion gap may coexist with low bicarbonate; The formula predicts pH but not the mechanism.

items.title: Anion gap: calculation and causes
items.contentHtml:
Anion gap (AG)

  • AG = sodium − (chlorine + bicarbonate); normal 8–12 mEq/L (without potassium).
  • Elevated AG (>12) indicates acidosis due to non-chlorinated acids: lactic, keto acids, renal failure, toxic (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates).
  • Normal AG (hyperchloremic) occurs due to loss of gastrointestinal (diarrhea) or renal bicarbonate (renal tubular acidosis), or due to chlorine intake (solution saline).
  • Albumin-corrected AG: Effective AG = measured AG + 2.5 × (normal albumin 4 − current albumin); Hypoalbuminemia masks elevated AG.
  • Useful to differentiate metabolic acidosis: elevated AG vs normal AG guides etiology.
  • Trap: in mixed disorder, AG can be elevated despite normal bicarbonate due to concomitant metabolic alkalosis.

items.title: Metabolic acidosis: etiologies
items.contentHtml:
Causes of metabolic acidosis

  • Classification by anion gap: elevated vs normal (hyperchloremic).
  • Elevated AG: diabetic ketoacidosis, fasting, alcohol; lactic acidosis (type A hypoxia, type B drugs); acute/chronic renal failure (sulfate/phosphate retention); toxic: methanol (formate), ethylene glycol (glycolate), paraldehyde, salicylates.
  • Normal GA: diarrhea (loss of bicarbonate), pancreatic/biliary fistulas, ureteroenterostomy, renal tubular acidosis (types 1, 2, 4), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide), hydrochloric acid or chloride ammonium.
  • Expected respiratory compensation: PaCO2 = 1.5 × bicarbonate + 8 ± 2 (Winters formula).
  • Threshold: if measured PaCO2 differs >2 mmHg from the expected → mixed disorder.
  • Trap: in lactic acidosis, AG may be normal if there is hypoalbuminemia; use corrected AG.

items.title: Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting
items.contentHtml:
Metabolic alkalosis due to vomiting

  • Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid → increased serum bicarbonate and low urinary chloride (<20 mEq/L).
  • Mechanisms: volume depletion activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system → sodium-potassium exchange, hypokalemia; Hypochloremia reduces renal excretion of bicarbonate.
  • Pathophysiology: loss of hydrogen ions and chlorine; the kidney retains bicarbonate to maintain electroneutrality.
  • Treatment: 0.9% saline intravenous + potassium replacement; responds to chlorine (chloro-sensitive).
  • If it does not respond to chlorine → suspect hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's syndrome, severe hypokalemia.
  • Trap: alkalosis due to vomiting can occur with alkaline pH but very high bicarbonate; blood gas analysis shows compensatory PaCO2 >45 mmHg.

items.title: Respiratory compensation
items.contentHtml:
Compensación respiratoria aguda vs crónica

  • Acidosis metabólica aguda: compensación hiperventilación ocurre en minutos; PaCO2 esperada = 1.5 × bicarbonato + 8 ± 2 (Winters).
  • Alcalosis metabólica: compensación hipoventilación; PaCO2 esperada = 0.7 × bicarbonato + 20 ± 5 (límite <55 mmHg).
  • Acidosis respiratoria aguda: bicarbonato aumenta 1 mEq/L por cada 10 mmHg de PaCO2 >40 (aguda); crónica: 3.5 mEq/L por cada 10 mmHg (compensación renal).
  • Alcalosis respiratoria aguda: bicarbonato disminuye 2 mEq/L por cada 10 mmHg de PaCO2 <40; crónica: 5 mEq/L por cada 10 mmHg.
  • Regla de oro: si la compensación excede los límites calculados → trastorno mixto.
  • Trampa: en EPOC crónico, PaCO2 alta con bicarbonato alto puede simular alcalosis metabólica; usar pH y historia.

items.title: Gasometría: pasos iniciales
items.contentHtml:
Initial interpretation of arterial blood gas

  • Step 1: evaluate pH: <7.35 acidosis, >7.45 alkalosis; normal 7.35–7.45.
  • Step 2: determine primary disorder: if low pH and high PaCO2 → respiratory acidosis; if low pH and low bicarbonate → metabolic acidosis; High pH and low PaCO2 → respiratory alkalosis; High pH and high bicarbonate → metabolic alkalosis.
  • Step 3: calculate expected compensation (Winters formulas or exchange rules for 10 mmHg).
  • Step 4: calculate anion gap (AG) and delta ratio if there is metabolic acidosis.
  • Step 5: verify oxygenation: PaO2 <60 mmHg in room air indicates hypoxemia; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300 → acute lung injury.
  • Trap: in mixed disorder, pH may be normal or almost normal; always compare with expected compensation.

items.title: Delta ratio: profit
items.contentHtml:
Delta ratio (Δ/Δ)

  • Fórmula: Δ/Δ = (AG actual − 12) / (24 − bicarbonato actual).
  • Interpretación: <1 → acidosis mixta AG normal (hiperclorémica) concomitante; 1–2 → acidosis AG pura; >2 → alcalosis metabólica concomitante.
  • Valor normal de AG 12 mEq/L y bicarbonato 24 mEq/L como referencia.
  • Útil para detectar trastornos mixtos en acidosis metabólica con AG elevado.
  • Ejemplo: cetoacidosis diabética con vómitos → Δ/Δ >2 por alcalosis metabólica añadida.
  • Trampa: si la acidosis es mixta (AG elevado + hiperclorémica), Δ/Δ <1; no asumir error de laboratorio.

items.title: Osmolar hiatus
items.contentHtml:
Osmolar hiatus in methanol poisoning

  • Osmolar hiatus = measured osmolarity − calculated osmolarity; normal <10 mOsm/kg.
  • Calculated osmolarity = 2 × sodium + glucose/18 + urea nitrogen/2.8 (in mg/dL) + ethanol/4.6 (if present).
  • Elevated osmolar hiatus (>10) suggests presence of toxic alcohol: methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropanol.
  • In methanol poisoning, the hiatus osmolar may be normal if metabolism has already converted methanol to formic acid (late phase); then metabolic acidosis with elevated AG predominates.
  • Differential diagnosis: ethylene glycol also causes osmolar hiatus and acidosis; oxalate crystals in urine lead to ethylene glycol.
  • Treatment: fomepizole (15 mg/kg intravenous) or ethanol; hemodialysis if severe acidosis or osmolar hiatus >50.

items.title: Distal TKA (type 1)
items.contentHtml:
Acidosis tubular renal distal (tipo 1)

  • Defecto en la secreción de hidrogeniones en el túbulo colector → incapacidad de acidificar orina (pH urinario >5.5) a pesar de acidosis sistémica.
  • Causa acidosis metabólica hiperclorémica con anión gap normal e hipocalemia.
  • Complicaciones: nefrolitiasis (cálculos de fosfato cálcico), nefrocalcinosis, osteomalacia.
  • Etiologías: autoimmune (síndrome de Sjögren, lupus), fármacos (anfotericina B, litio), hipercalcemia, obstructivas.
  • Diagnóstico: test de acidificación con cloruro de amonio; si pH urinario no baja <5.3 → distal.
  • Tratamiento: bicarbonato de sodio oral 1–3 mEq/kg/día; corregir hipocalemia antes de alcalinizar para evitar arritmias.

items.title: Respiratory alkalosis
items.contentHtml:
Respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation

  • Definition: pH >7.45 with PaCO2 <35 mmHg and normal or low bicarbonate.
  • Causes: anxiety, pain, hypoxemia, sepsis, liver failure, salicylate poisoning, pregnancy, fever.
  • Renal compensation: excretion of bicarbonate; acute: 2 mEq/L decrease for every 10 mmHg of low PaCO2; chronic: 5 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg.
  • Symptoms: paresthesias, tetany, carpopedal spasm due to transient hypocalcemia (alkalosis reduces ionized calcium).
  • Treatment of the underlying cause; do not use a paper bag in hypoxemia or sepsis.
  • Trap: in salicylate poisoning, the initial respiratory alkalosis can progress to mixed metabolic acidosis; measure levels.

items.title: Base excess (BE)
items.contentHtml:
Base excess and bicarbonate deficiency

  • Base excess (BE) is the amount of acid or base necessary to titrate 1 L of blood to pH 7.40 with PaCO2 of 40 mmHg at 37°C.
  • Normal BE: −2 to +2 mEq/L; negative indicates base deficit (metabolic acidosis), positive excess (metabolic alkalosis).
  • Bicarbonate deficit (in mEq) = weight (kg) × 0.4 × (desired bicarbonate − current bicarbonate) for metabolic acidosis.
  • Correction: administer half the deficit as a bolus, then reevaluate; avoid overcorrection.
  • BE is useful to quantify severity and guide replacement in arrest or shock.
  • Trap: BE does not differentiate respiratory from metabolic causes; always correlate with pH and PaCO2.

items.foco: Trastorno mixto: pH, PaCO2 y HCO3
items.title: Mixed disorders
items.contentHtml:
Trastorno mixto

  • Definición: presencia de dos o más trastornos primarios simultáneos; ejemplos: acidosis metabólica + acidosis respiratoria (paro), acidosis metabólica + alcalosis respiratoria (sepsis).
  • Diagnóstico: comparar PaCO2 y bicarbonato con compensación esperada; si no coinciden → mixto.
  • pH puede ser normal, extremo o inapropiadamente normal; siempre calcular anión gap y delta ratio.
  • Ejemplo: acidosis metabólica con AG elevado + alcalosis metabólica → pH puede ser normal, AG >12, delta ratio >2.
  • Ejemplo: acidosis respiratoria crónica + acidosis metabólica → bicarbonato menor que el esperado para la PaCO2.
  • Trampa: en trastorno mixto, la compensación nunca debe ser perfecta; si pH es normal pero hay anión gap alto, buscar mixto.
